topic.claim: When your mother asks what something cost, you halve the price. It isn't a lie; it's a currency conversion that spares her the worry.

paragraphs: When mummy asks "kitne ka liya?", you say half the price.
That isn't a lie. It's a currency conversion.
You hear yourself say "₹5,000, sale tha."
You didn't plan it. It just came out.
She hears what ₹12,000 meant in the years she ran the house on one salary, counting every note before the month ended.
So the real number isn't a price to her. It's a worry.
Is the child saving anything? Who taught them to spend like this?
Halving the price is how you take that worry off her.
You're not hiding the sneakers. You're hiding what that number does to her.
She knows this trick, because she plays it on you.
Ask what her last saree cost.
Two people in one house, both halving prices,
so nobody has to worry about the other.

claims.text: India's Time Use Survey found women who did unpaid domestic work spent about 289-299 minutes a day on it (2024 and 2019 rounds); men about 88-97 minutes.

draft.search_phrase: lying to your parents about prices

ledger.text: A parent who ran a household on one tight income reflexively measures any price a child states against what that sum once cost her in effort and sacrifice rather than against the number itself, reads a high price as evidence of carelessness and starts worrying, and so the child states a lower price not to deceive but to prevent that worry — making the understatement a protective act rather than a lie.
ledger.sentence: Because mummy doesn't hear ₹12,000. She hears what ₹12,000 meant in the years she ran the house on one salary, counting every note before the month ended. So the real number isn't a price to her. It's a worry. ... Halving the price is how you take that worry off her. You're not hiding the sneakers. You're hiding what that number does to her.

mechanism.actual_mechanism: The post makes no falsifiable claim about how a price, fee, tax, contract or market works. Its load-bearing claims are all readings of motive and emotion — that a parent measures a stated price against her own past sacrifice, reads a high number as worry rather than data, and that the child understates to spare her that worry. These are interpretations of a moment and generalizations about family life, not statements about mechanisms that can be checked against primary sources. The one concrete step described — stating ₹5,000 instead of ₹12,000 — is a plain halving and is internally consistent.

alt_texts: When mummy asks "kitne ka liya?", you say half the price. That isn't a lie. It's a currency conversion.
The sneakers cost ₹12,000. You hear yourself say "₹5,000, sale tha." You didn't plan it. It just came out.
Because mummy doesn't hear ₹12,000. She hears what ₹12,000 meant in the years she ran the house on one salary, counting every note before the month ended.
So the real number isn't a price to her. It's a worry. Is the child saving anything? Who taught them to spend like this?
Halving the price is how you take that worry off her. You're not hiding the sneakers. You're hiding what that number does to her.
She knows this trick, because she plays it on you. Ask what her last saree cost. "Arre, sasta tha." It wasn't.
Two people in one house, both halving prices, so nobody has to worry about the other.

history.point: You and your mother both lie about prices to each other, not to deceive but to protect the other from worrying about money.
history.reason: Because to her the real price isn't just a number, it brings back the years she ran the house alone counting every rupee, so a high number becomes a worry instead of a fact.
ideas: halving prices is how you protect your mother from money-worry, and she does the same for you
